'''''Tragopogon porrifolius''''' is a species of plant commonly known as '''purple''' or '''common salsify''', '''oyster plant''', '''vegetable oyster''', '''Jerusalem star''',<ref name=unl>{{ cite web |url=http://www.unl.edu/agnicpls/gpcn/gpcnj.html |work=Historical Common Names of Great Plains Plants |title=''J'' |publisher=[[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] |access-date=March 9, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091207085100/http://www.unl.edu/agnicpls/gpcn/gpcnj.html |archive-date=December 7, 2009 }}</ref> '''Jack go to bed''',<ref name=storl>{{cite book |last1=Storl |first1=Wolf-Dieter |title=Bekannte und vergessene Gemüse: Ethnobotanik, Heilkunde und Anwendungen |date=2012 |publisher=AT Verlag |location=Aarau |isbn=978-3-03800-672-5}}</ref> '''goatsbeard''',<ref name=Audubon>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |author-link1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=404}}</ref> or simply '''salsify'''. These last two names are also applied to other species. 

It grows wild in many places and is one of the most widely known species of the salsify genus, ''[[Tragopogon]]''. It is cultivated for its ornamental [[flower]] and [[edible root]].

==Description==
The plant grows to {{cvt|1.2|m|ft|0}} in height.<ref name="auduflo">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/403/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |pages=403–404 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> As with other ''Tragopogon'' species, its stem is largely unbranched and the leaves are somewhat grasslike, up to {{Convert|30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long.<ref name="auduflo" /> It exudes a milky juice from the stems. The taproots can become {{Convert|15–30|cm|abbr=on|frac=2}} long and {{Convert|2-5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} thick.<ref name="seedSav">{{cite book |last1=Heistinger |first1=Andrea |title=The manual of seed saving: harvesting, storing and sowing techniques for vegetables, herbs and fruits |date=2013 |publisher=Timber Press Portland |isbn=978-1-60469-382-9 |location=London}}</ref>

It typically flowers from June to September,<ref name="auduflo" /> but in warmer areas such as [[California]] it can be found in bloom from April. The [[flower head]] is purple and {{cvt|5-7.5|cm|4=0}} across and each is surrounded by 8–9 tapered bracts<ref name="auduflo" /> which are longer than the petals (technically, the [[ligule]]s of the ray flowers). The flowers are [[hermaphrodite|hermaphroditic]] and [[pollinated by insects]].

The fruits are beaked [[achene]]s, rod-shaped with light ribs. They have hairs at one end that facilitate wind dispersal.<ref name=hei10>{{cite book |last1=Heistinger |first1=Andrea |last2=Lerch |first2=Franziska |title=Handbuch Bio-Gemüse: Sortenvielfalt für den eigenen Garten |date=2010 |publisher=Ulmer |isbn=978-3-8001-6950-4}}</ref> The achenes are 10–17 mm long and 1–3 mm wide without counting the beak, which is up to 55 mm in length.<ref name= seedSav /> When the fruits are formed fully, the hairs from the fruits give the appearance of a ball of fluff which gives the plant its name "goatsbeard".<ref name=Audubon/>

''[[Tragopogon pratensis]]'' has similar but smaller flowers.

== Etymology ==
The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''porrifolius'' means "with leaves like [[leek]]" (''Allium porrum'').<ref name="RHSLG">{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |year=2012 |isbn=978-1-84533-731-5 |location=United Kingdom}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Tragopogon porrifolius'' is a common [[Biennial plant|biennial]] wildflower, native to southeast Europe, Mediterranean Turkey, and north Africa,<ref name="seedSav" /> but [[introduced species|introduced]] elsewhere, for example, into the [[British Isles]] (mainly in central and southern England),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Stace |first=Clive |author-link=Clive Stace |title=New Flora of the British Isles |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-521-70772-5 |edition=3rd |location=Cambridge, UK}} p. 707.</ref> other parts of northern Europe, [[North America]] and southern [[Africa]], and in Australia. In the United States, it is now found growing wild in almost every state, including [[Hawaii]], except in the extreme south-east.

== Cultivation ==
The root and the young [[Shoot (botany)|shoot]]s of ''T. porrifolius'' can be eaten (after being boiled).<ref>{{cite book |last=Lyons |first=C. P. |author-link=C. P. Lyons |title=Trees, Shrubs and Flowers to Know in Washington |date=1956 |publisher=J. M. Dent & Sons |location=Canada |pages=153, 196 |edition=1st}}</ref> The freshly grown leaves can be eaten cooked or raw.<ref name = seedSav/><ref name=Audubon/> Historically, the plant was cultivated for that purpose; it is mentioned by classical authors such as [[Pliny the Elder]]. Cultivation in Europe began in the 16th century in [[France]] and [[Italy]]. In the United Kingdom it was initially grown for its flower and later became a mildly popular vegetable in the 18th century but then declined in popularity. Presently the root is cultivated and eaten most frequently in France, Germany, Italy and [[Russia]]. However, in modern times it has tended to be replaced by [[Spanish salsify]] (''Scorzonera hispanica'') as a cultivated crop.

Cultivated varieties include 'White French', 'Gian French',<ref name=storl/> 'Mammoth Sandwich Island',<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Lloyd|first=John W.|date=February 1902|title=Vegetables for a farmer's garden in northern Illinois|url=https://www.ideals.illinois.edu/bitstream/handle/2142/33678/5230821.pdf?sequence=2|journal=University of Illinois: Agricultural Experiment Station|volume=Circular No. 45|pages=1–5}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal|last=Andersen|first=Craig R.|date=7 July 2011|title=Home Gardening Series: Salsify|url=https://www.uaex.edu/publications/PDF/FSA-6094.pdf|journal=Agriculture and Natural Resources|via=Elsevier}}</ref> 'Improved Mammoth Sandwich Island', 'Blauetikett',<ref name=storl/> and 'Lüthy';<ref name=storl/> they are generally characterised by larger or better-shaped roots. To maintain the purity of the cultivar a distance of 500 ft (150 m) has to be met. When ''T. porrifolius'' is grown for seed, it is harvested in the second season from midsummer to early autumn to select for bolt resistance.<ref name=seedSav/> The root becomes discoloured and spoils quickly if broken, which can easily happen since it is difficult to remove from the soil without damage.

===Sowing and soil requirements===
Salsify is grown similarly to other root vegetables like [[parsnip]] and [[carrot]]s and thus requires similar attention.<ref name=":12" /><ref name=":22">{{Cite journal|last=BosweII|first=Victor R.|date=1957|title=Vegetables|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AmDYL4i4vRkC&q=Victor+R.+BosweII+1957&pg=PA692|journal=Yearbook of Agriculture|pages=692–698}}</ref> [[Sowing]] can be done in late summer or early winter<ref name=":12" /> to foster an early growth.<ref name=":0" /> Planting can also be done in early spring about 100 days before the first frosts in a well prepared soil, preferably a [[loam]] or [[Silt loam|silt-loam]].<ref name=":22" /> It should be done at the depth of 1.3 to 2 cm. Spacing between rows should be around 45 to 60 cm and the seeds should be separated by 3 cm approximately. This represent 12 g of seeds per 10 m of row for the cultivar 'Mammoth Sandwich Island'. A thinning to 5 cm between the plants is needed when the seedlings reach 5 cm.<ref name=":12" /> ''T. porrifolius'' needs deep and loose soils which are not too dry for a good development of the taproot. Stony or waterlogged soils have negative effects on yields and hamper harvesting. Other root crops, legumes and cereals have been mentioned as possible preculture. ''T. porrifolius'' is a moderate feeder, therefore the application of fresh manure does not improve yields. During the main growing period a good water supply prevents potential branching of the taproot.<ref name=bisa>{{cite book |last1=Dachler |first1=Michael |title=Bildatlas Samen: Getreide, Pseudocerealien, Gemüse, Ölpflanzen, Eiweißpflanzen, Grünlandpflanzen, Gründüngung, Faserpflanzen, Farbstoffpflanzen, Arzneipflanzen, Gewürzpflanzen. |date=2017 |publisher=DLG-Verlag |location=Frankfurt am Main |isbn=978-3-7690-0845-6}}</ref>

===Climate requirements===
There are no specific requirements known for the cultivation of ''T. porrifolius'', but they have been successfully cultivated in temperate climate zones.<ref name=hei10/> The seedlings need a temperature of 8–16 °C to germinate and the plant will freeze between −1.1 and −1.6 °C. ''T. porrifolius'' can cope with low temperatures and is not injured by light freezing.<ref name=bisa/><ref name=nep>{{cite book |last1=Joshi |first1=Bal Krishna |last2=Shrestha |first2=Renuka |title=Working Groups of Agricultural PlantGenetic Resources (APGRs) in Nepal. Proceedings of National Workshop, 21−22 June 2018, Kathmandu |publisher=National Agriculture Genetic Resources Center |isbn=978-9937-0-6000-4 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/334052118 |access-date=20 November 2019}}</ref>

===Growth and development===
The seeds need 8–10 days of germination time. ''T. porrifolius'' is a biennial plant. In the first year only the vegetative parts of the plant are developed. In autumn, the energy is stored in the root system, which is depending on the variety more or less branched. In the second season the generative purple flowers evolve.<ref name="bisa" /> They bloom from early to mid summer.<ref name="hei10" />

===Harvest and storage===
The taproots are usually harvested from late autumn onwards (later than October in the Northern Hemisphere) and during winter. Harvesting after a frost is favoured to improve the taste of the root. After flowering, the taproot becomes stringy and inedible.<ref name=bisa/> The taproots can be stored in traditional [[Storage clamp|clamps]] although refrigerated storage has been recommended at 0 °C and 90–95% relative humidity for 2–4 months.<ref name=hei10/><ref name=nep/>

===Pests and diseases===
Few pests or diseases affect ''T. porrifolius''. White rust (''[[Albugo tragopogonis]]'') is the most common disease. Closely related wild species (e.g. ''[[Tragopogon pratensis]]''), black salsify (''[[Scorzonera hispanica]]''), gerbera (''[[Gerbera]]'') and sunflower (''[[Helianthus annuus]]'') are also found to be hosts of this fungus. At an early stage chlorotic spotting is visible on leaves and stems. These develop during the course of disease into small white blisters.

Occasional problems are reported with [[Rust (fungus)|rust]] diseases caused by ''[[Puccinia hystericum]]'', ''[[Puccinia jackyana]]'' and ''[[Puccinia scorzonera]]''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Thompson |first1=Anthony Keith |title=Fruit and vegetables: harvesting, handling and storage |date=2015 |publisher=Wiley-Blackwell |location=Chichester |isbn=978-1-118-65404-0 |edition=Third |oclc=904730845 }}</ref> Mulching with oats and the use of spring vetch (''[[Vicia sativa]]'') or blue tansy (''[[Phacelia tanacetifolia]]'') as cover crops reduces the number of fungi infecting seedlings and roots. The following fungi have been isolated from ''T. porrifolius'' seedlings and roots: ''[[Alternaria alternata]]'', ''[[Fusarium culmorum]]'', ''[[Fusarium oxysporum]]'', ''[[Penicillium]]'' spp., ''[[Rhizoctonia solani]]'' and ''[[Sclerotinia sclerotiorum]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Clements |first1=David R. |last2=Upadhyaya |first2=Mahesh K. |last3=Bos |first3=Shelley J. |title=The biology of Canadian weeds. 110. Tragopogon dubius Scop., Tragopogon pratensis L., and Tragopogon porrifolius L. |journal=Canadian Journal of Plant Science |date=1999 |volume=79 |issue=1 |pages=153–163 |doi=10.4141/P98-007 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

When the rows are planted too close together, powdery mildew (''[[Erysiphe cichoriacearum]]'') can affect the plants.<ref name=nep/>

When the roots are left in the ground over winter, mice and voles may nibble them.<ref name=nep/>

== Uses ==
A [[latex]] derived from the root can be used as a [[chewing gum]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}}

===As food===
The plant is edible,<ref>{{Cite book|last=Fagan|first=Damian|title=Wildflowers of Oregon: A Field Guide to Over 400 Wildflowers, Trees, and Shrubs of the Coast, Cascades, and High Desert|publisher=[[FalconGuides]]|year=2019|isbn=978-1-4930-3633-2|location=Guilford, CT|page=161|oclc=1073035766}}</ref> but the roots and leaves are most palatable when collected before the flower stalk is produced.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last1=Elias|first1=Thomas S.|title=Edible Wild Plants: A North American Field Guide to Over 200 Natural Foods|last2=Dykeman|first2=Peter A.|publisher=[[Sterling Publishing|Sterling]]|year=2009|isbn=978-1-4027-6715-9|location=New York|page=112|oclc=244766414|orig-date=1982}}</ref> The root is noted for having a mild taste when uncooked, described as like asparagus or [[oyster]]s, from which the plant derives its alternative name of oyster plant. The outer layers can be scraped off, with the root dipped in cold water to preserve its colour.<ref name=":1" /> If too tough for eating, they can be boiled with a pinch of baking soda and a change of water.<ref name=":1" /> Raw young roots can be grated for use in salads, but older roots are better cooked. They can be added to soups, stews or stir-fries. Salsify [[purée]] (alone or including potato) is recommended with fish.<ref name="Special Fruit">{{cite web |title=Salsify |url=https://www.specialfruit.com/en/products/detail/salsify/nzffz |website=Special Fruit NV |access-date=10 November 2020}}</ref>

The flowering shoots can be used like [[asparagus]], either raw or cooked and the flowers can be added to salad, while the sprouted seeds can be used in salads or sandwiches.

Raw salsify is 77% water, 19% [[carbohydrate]]s, 3% [[protein (nutrient)|protein]] and contains negligible [[fat]]. In a 100 gram reference amount, raw salsify supplies 82 [[calorie]]s and moderate contents of [[riboflavin]], [[vitamin B6]], [[vitamin C]], [[manganese]] and [[phosphorus]].

==Phytochemicals==
''Tragopogon porrifolius'' contains [[polyphenol]] [[phytochemical]]s which are under preliminary research for their potential biological effects.<ref name="spina">{{Cite journal|last1=Spina|first1=Michele|last2=Cuccioloni|first2=Massimiliano|last3=Sparapani|first3=Luca|last4=Acciarri|first4=Stefano|last5=Eleuteri|first5=Anna Maria|last6=Fioretti|first6=Evandro|last7=Angeletti|first7=Mauro|date=2008|title=Comparative evaluation of flavonoid content in assessing quality of wild and cultivated vegetables for human consumption|journal=[[Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture]]|language=en|volume=88|issue=2|pages=294–304|doi=10.1002/jsfa.3089|issn=1097-0010}}</ref> ''Tragopogon'' species are being studied at the [[biochemistry|biochemical level]] for their novel [[enzyme]] forms and [[Gene polymorphism|genetic polymorphism]].<ref name="Soltis">{{cite journal | last1=Soltis | first1=Pamela S. | last2=Liu | first2=Xiaoxian | last3=Marchant | first3=D. Blaine | last4=Visger | first4=Clayton J. | last5=Soltis | first5=Douglas E. | title=Polyploidy and novelty: Gottlieb's legacy | journal=[[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences]]| volume=369 | issue=1648 | date=5 August 2014 | issn=0962-8436 | doi=10.1098/rstb.2013.0351 | article-number=20130351|pmid=24958924|pmc=4071524}}</ref>
